title.text: Probability basics: random variables, expectation, variance and covariance

objects.text: A chat model gives every possible next word a probability. What does that number mean, and why do they all add up to exactly one?

Mathematics for AI and Machine Learning  |  Session 13 of 18  |  Probability and statistics
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes: Welcome to Session 13, and to the third pillar of the course: probability and statistics. Everything so far gave us numbers. Now we deal with chance, which is what a language model faces every time it must pick the next word. Today is the vocabulary: random variables, expectation, variance and covariance. We use dice, a small next-word list and a small dataset.

objects.text: By the end of today you can

slides.notes:
Here is what you take away today. You can describe a sample space, an event and a random variable, and you can use the rules of probability on dice. You can calculate an expectation, a variance, a standard deviation, a covariance and a correlation, first by hand and then by computer.

And you can read the list of next-word probabilities that a chat model produces as a probability mass function. That last one answers the question on the first slide.

Your two hours: dice and data

We start with ten minutes of recall from Session 12, and the question about next-word probabilities. Then thirty-five minutes of concepts, always a picture first and then one example by hand. title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  Why can computing e to the power of a large score break a softmax, and what does the stable softmax do about it?
2.  What does regularisation (an L2 penalty, also called weight decay) add to the loss, and why?
3.  Many models use 16-bit numbers. What is the saving and what is the risk?

objects.alt: Three questions

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 12. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. Why can computing e to the power of a large score break a softmax, and what does the stable softmax do about it? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. The number overflows (too large for the computer). The stable softmax subtracts the largest score first. The probabilities stay the same.

Question two. What does regularisation (an L2 penalty, also called weight decay) add to the loss, and why? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. A penalty that grows with the size of the weights. It keeps weights small and reduces overfitting.

Question three. Many models use 16-bit numbers. What is the saving and what is the risk? Think about your own task as you answer.

A good answer is this. Less memory and less time. The largest number in the 16-bit floating-point format fp16 is only 65,504, so overflow comes sooner (bfloat16 keeps the range but loses precision).

If an answer was missing, do not worry. Your notes from last class have it. Now to today.

title.text: Answers to the three questions from Session 12

rows.text: Why can computing e to the power of a large score break a softmax, and what does the stable softmax do about it?
The number overflows (too large for the computer). The stable softmax subtracts the largest score first. The probabilities stay the same.
What does regularisation (an L2 penalty, also called weight decay) add to the loss, and why?
A penalty that grows with the size of the weights. It keeps weights small and reduces overfitting.
Many models use 16-bit numbers. What is the saving and what is the risk?
Less memory and less time. The largest number in the 16-bit floating-point format fp16 is only 65,504, so overflow comes sooner (bfloat16 keeps the range but loses precision).

objects.text: If one answer surprised you, look back at Session 12 before the lab.

slides.notes:
Here are the short answers. First, a large score overflows when we take e to its power. The stable softmax subtracts the largest score first, and the probabilities do not change. Second, regularisation adds a penalty that grows with the weights, so they stay small and overfitting is reduced.

Third, 16-bit numbers save memory and time, but in the fp16 format they top out at 65,504, so overflow comes sooner and the stable softmax matters more. The bfloat16 format keeps the range but loses precision. Check your own answers against these.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: A rule that turns the outcome of a chance event into a number. We write it X.
Probability mass function (pmf) and density function (pdf)
The pmf gives P(X = x) for discrete values (values you can list, such as the faces 1 to 6). The pdf is a curve, and probability is the area under it.
The probability-weighted average of X, written E(X) or mu.
The average squared distance from mu, and its square root sigma.
How two columns move together, and the same thing scaled to lie between -1 and +1.

objects.alt: question
chart

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Random variable. A rule that turns the outcome of a chance event into a number. We write it X.

Probability mass function (pmf) and density function (pdf). The pmf gives P(X = x) for discrete values (values you can list, such as the faces 1 to 6). The pdf is a curve, and probability is the area under it.

Expectation. The probability-weighted average of X, written E(X) or mu.

Variance and standard deviation. The average squared distance from mu, and its square root sigma.

Covariance and correlation. How two columns move together, and the same thing scaled to lie between -1 and +1.

title.text:
A sample space lists every outcome,
and an event is a group of outcomes

objects.alt: A sample space lists every outcome, and an event is a group of outcomes

objects.text: Two fair dice give 36 equally likely outcomes. Each cell shows the sum.

runs.text: Sample space: the set of all possible outcomes.
Event: a group of outcomes we care about. Gold = the event "sum is 7".

slides.notes:
Roll two fair dice. Each cell in this table is one outcome, and the number inside is the sum of the two dice. There are thirty-six cells, and they are equally likely. The set of all outcomes is called the sample space. An event is any group of outcomes we care about.

The gold cells are the event: the sum is seven. Six cells are gold out of thirty-six, so the probability is six over thirty-six, which is one sixth, about 0.167. Count the cells for the event "the sum is 10". What do you get?

title.text:
Probability is a number from 0 to 1, and
all the outcomes together add up to 1

objects.alt: Probability is a number from 0 to 1, and all the outcomes together add up to 1

objects.text: Probability P(A) measures how likely an event A is.

runs.text: 0 means impossible. 1 means certain.
For equally likely outcomes: P(A) = outcomes in A divided by all outcomes.
The probabilities of all the outcomes add up to 1.

slides.notes:
A probability is a number between zero and one. Zero means the event cannot happen, and one means it is certain. When all outcomes are equally likely, the probability of an event is the number of outcomes in it, divided by the number of all outcomes. Here is one fair die.

Six faces, each with probability one sixth. And the six bars together add up to exactly one, because something must happen when you roll. Hold on to that last sentence. It is the answer to our question from the first slide.

title.text: The rules of probability, checked on dice

objects.alt: The rules of probability, checked on dice

rows.text: Two events. A = the die is even {2, 4, 6}. B = the die shows more than 4 {5, 6}.
Both at once: only the face 6.
At least one: 2, 4, 5, 6. The 6 is counted once, so we subtract it once.

objects.text: Complement example: P(not even) = 1 - 3/6 = 3/6.

slides.notes:
Here are the four rules, and each one is checked on a single die. The probability is never below zero or above one. All outcomes together have probability one. The probability that A does not happen is one minus the probability that it does. And for either one of two events, add their probabilities and subtract the overlap, because the overlap was counted twice.

Take A as even and B as more than four. The six belongs to both, so three sixths plus two sixths minus one sixth gives four sixths. Check by listing 2, 4, 5, 6.

title.text:
A random variable turns each outcome into a
number, and its pmf says how likely each number is

objects.alt: A random variable turns each outcome into a number, and its pmf says how likely each number is

objects.text: Let X be the sum of two dice. The bar heights are the probability mass function (pmf): p(x) = P(X = x).

runs.text: A random variable X gives a number to each outcome.
P(X = 7) = 6/36 is the tallest bar (gold).
All the bars add up to 1.

slides.notes:
A random variable is a rule that gives a number to every outcome of a chance event. Here X is the sum of two dice, so X can be any whole number from two to twelve. The heights of the bars are the probability mass function, the pmf: for each value x, the probability that X equals x.

Seven is the tallest because six of the thirty-six outcomes give it. Two and twelve are the shortest, one outcome each. Add all eleven bars and you get thirty-six over thirty-six, which is one. What is P(X = 2)?

title.text:
A continuous random variable has a density
curve, and probability is the area under it

objects.alt: A continuous random variable has a density curve, and probability is the area under it

objects.text: A bus arrives at a random moment in a 10 minute window. This is a uniform distribution: every moment is equally likely.

runs.text: Density f(x) (pdf): the curve, flat at 1/10 = 0.1, so total area = 10 × 0.1 = 1.
P(2 to 5 minutes) = width 3 × height 0.1 = 0.3.
P(exactly 3.000...) = 0. Only ranges have probability.

slides.notes:
Now a random variable whose values cannot be listed. The waiting time for a bus, in a ten minute window, can be any value, so we call it continuous. For these we cannot list bars. Instead we draw a density curve, the probability density function, the pdf. The height of the curve is not a probability.

The area under the curve between two values is. Here the curve is flat at 0.1, so the area between two and five minutes is three times 0.1, which is 0.3. The probability of one exact instant is zero. This flat curve is called a uniform distribution: every moment in the ten minutes is equally likely, so the height is one tenth and the total area is ten times 0.1, which is one. These numbers are illustrative, made up to show the arithmetic.

title.text:
Probability mass function and
density function, side by side

objects.alt: Probability mass function and density function, side by side

rows.text: The probability that X takes exactly the value x. Never negative.
The density: the height of the curve at x. It can be above 1.
Add the probabilities of every possible value x.
The area under the curve from a to b. Here we read it as width times height.

objects.text: Both say the same thing: the total probability is 1. Discrete values use a sum, a continuous curve uses an area.

slides.notes:
Here are the two descriptions side by side. For discrete values, which you can list, we have the pmf, written p of x, which is the probability that X equals x, and the sum over all values must be one. For a continuous variable we have the density f of x, and the probability that X lies between a and b is the area under the curve from a to b.

That area symbol is called an integral. You do not need to calculate integrals by hand in this course. For flat curves it is width times height. The total area under the whole curve must also be one.

title.text:
A chat model gives every possible next word
a probability, and the probabilities add up to 1

objects.alt: A chat model gives every possible next word a probability, and the probabilities add up to 1

objects.text: Illustrative (made-up numbers): next word after "For breakfast I drink hot ...".

runs.text: Logits z: one raw score per word.
Softmax turns the scores into probabilities.

slides.notes:
This is the answer to our question, with made-up numbers, so please treat them as illustrative. Suppose a model reads the start of a sentence, and it scores five candidate next words. These raw scores are called logits. Softmax, which you met in Session 12, turns them into probabilities.

Tea gets 0.446, coffee 0.299, and so on. This list is a probability mass function. It is never negative, and it adds up to one, because the model must choose some word. A real model does this for every token in its vocabulary. Which word would you bet on?

title.text:
Expectation is the probability-weighted
average, the balance point of the bars

objects.alt: Expectation is the probability-weighted average, the balance point of the bars

objects.text: Expectation E(X), also called the mean and written mu, is the value the average settles on over many repeats.

runs.text: Picture the bars as weights on a ruler. E(X) is where it balances.
It need not be a possible value: no die shows 3.5.

slides.notes:
Expectation answers the question: what would the average be if we repeated this chance event many times?

Imagine the bars as weights on a ruler. The expectation is the point where the ruler balances. For a fair die it is exactly in the middle, 3.5. Notice that you can never roll a 3.5. The expectation is an average over many rolls and says nothing certain about one roll.

Statisticians also call it the mean and write it mu. If the bars were not equal, which way would the balance point move?

title.text:
Expectation: add up each
value times its probability

objects.alt: Expectation: add up each value times its probability

rows.text: The expectation (mean) of the random variable X.
One possible value of X, and its probability.
Add the products x times p(x) over all values.

objects.text: Next-word example (illustrative): lengths 3, 6, 5, 4, 4 letters give E(length) = 4.30 letters.

slides.notes:
The formula says: multiply each possible value by its probability, and add. For the die each face has probability one sixth, so we get twenty-one sixths, which is 3.5. The same formula works on any pmf. Take our five next words, with lengths of three, six, five, four and four letters.

Weight each length by its probability and you get 4.30 letters. That is the expected length of the next word, in the toy model. Try the first two terms yourself: three times 0.446, plus six times 0.299.

title.text:
Variance and standard deviation measure
how far values lie from the mean

objects.alt: Variance and standard deviation measure how far values lie from the mean

rows.text: Variance: average squared distance from mu (units of X squared).
Standard deviation: the square root, in the units of X.
How far one value lies from the expectation.
The expectation of X squared: sum of x squared times p(x).

objects.text: We square the distances so that below-mean and above-mean values do not cancel.

slides.notes:
Expectation tells us the centre. Variance tells us the spread. For each value take its distance from the mean, square it, weight it by its probability, and add. We square so that values below and above the mean do not cancel each other. The standard deviation, sigma, is the square root of the variance, and it has the same units as X, which makes it easier to read.

There is also a shortcut: the expectation of X squared, minus mu squared. For the die the expectation of X squared is 91 over 6, which is 15.1667, minus 12.25, and both routes give 2.9167. Next we do it by hand.

title.text:
By hand: the variance of a
fair die is 35/12, about 2.92

objects.alt: By hand: the variance of a fair die is 35/12, about 2.92

objects.text: Each face has p(x) = 1/6, so add the last column and divide by 6.

runs.text: Sum of the last column = 17.50.
Standard deviation = square root = 1.7078.

slides.notes:
Let us do the die by hand. Column one is the face. Column two is its distance from 3.5, and column three squares that distance. The ends, 1 and 6, are 2.5 away, and squared that gives 6.25. The middle faces are only half a unit away, which gives 0.25.

Add the six squared distances and you get 17.5. Every face has probability one sixth, so divide by six. The variance is 2.9167, and the standard deviation is 1.7078. A typical roll lands about 1.7 away from 3.5.

title.text:
Covariance asks whether two
columns rise and fall together

objects.alt: Covariance asks whether two columns rise and fall together

objects.text: Illustrative data: six learners. Dashed red lines mark the two means. Shaded corners are marked +.

runs.text: Dark dot: both above or both below the means. Product positive.
Open dot: product negative.
Per learner: (x - mean of x) times (y - mean of y). Covariance = mean of these products.

slides.notes:
Now two columns at once. Here are six learners, with the hours they study per week on the horizontal axis and the quiz score on the vertical axis. These numbers are illustrative. The two dashed lines are the means, and they cut the picture into four corners. A dark dot sits in the top right or bottom left corner, which means both values are above or both below average.

Those dots add positive amounts to the covariance. For each learner we multiply the distance from the mean of x by the distance from the mean of y, and the covariance is the mean of those products. An open dot sits in the other corners and pulls it down. Most dots here are dark, so the covariance is positive.

title.text:
By hand: the covariance of the
six learners is 25/6, about 4.167

objects.alt: By hand: the covariance of the six learners is 25/6, about 4.167

objects.text: The means are 4 hours and 6 points. Multiply the two distances for every learner.

runs.text: Covariance = 25 / 6 = 4.1667.
Variance of x = 4.6667. Variance of y = 7.

slides.notes:
Here is the hand calculation. The mean of x is four hours and the mean of y is six points. For each learner we take the distance from each mean and multiply the two. The first learner is three below on hours and two below on score, so the product is plus six.

The third learner studied little but scored high, so the product is minus two. The six products add to 25, and 25 over 6 is 4.1667. That is the covariance. Because two products are negative, the answer is smaller than if all had moved together.

title.text:
Covariance and correlation: how
two columns move together

objects.alt: Covariance and correlation: how two columns move together

rows.text: The mean of the products of the two distances.
Covariance divided by both standard deviations. No units, between -1 and +1. (rho: same, for a population.)

objects.text: This course divides by n (population form). Cov of a column with itself is its variance.

slides.notes:
Here are the two formulas. Covariance is the average of the products of the distances from the means. The rho symbol is the same quantity for a whole population, and r is the one computed from data. Its units are the units of x times the units of y, so here hours times points, which is hard to interpret.

Correlation fixes that. Divide the covariance by both standard deviations and the units cancel. The result always lies between minus one and plus one. For our six learners it is 0.729: a fairly strong positive link. Notice a useful fact. The covariance of a column with itself is its variance.

title.text:
Correlation runs from -1 to +1, and
it only sees straight-line patterns

objects.alt: Correlation runs from -1 to +1, and it only sees straight-line patterns

objects.text: Each panel shows 40 made-up points and their correlation r.

runs.text: r near +1: the columns rise together.
r near -1: one rises as the other falls.
r near 0: no straight-line trend.

slides.notes:
Here is correlation as a picture. Forty made-up points in each panel. On the left the columns move in opposite directions, so r is close to minus one. In the middle the dots form a cloud with no trend, and r is near zero. On the right they rise together and r is close to plus one.

Correlation is a single number that summarises the straight-line trend. That is useful, and it is also its limit, as the picture after this one shows.

title.text:
Common mistake: a correlation near 0
does not mean the columns are unrelated

objects.alt: Common mistake: a correlation near 0 does not mean the columns are unrelated

objects.text: Both panels have r close to 0. Only the right one has no relationship.

runs.text: Correlation measures straight-line trends only.
A strong curve can still give r near 0.
High correlation does not prove that one column causes the other.

slides.notes:
A common mistake. Both of these panels have a correlation near zero. The right panel is a cloud with no pattern. The left panel has a perfect U shape, a very strong relationship, but not a straight line. Correlation cannot see curves. So always draw the scatter plot before you trust the number.

And one more caution. Even a high correlation does not show that one column causes the other. Ice cream sales and sunburn both rise in summer. Which hidden factor links them?

title.text:
Two versions of variance: divide
by n or divide by n minus 1

objects.alt: check

objects.text: Population: divide by n

runs.text: VAR.P, COVARIANCE.P
np.var, np.cov(bias=True)
This course uses this version

objects.alt: flag

objects.text: Sample: divide by n - 1

runs.text: VAR.S, COVARIANCE.S
pandas .var(), .cov()
Used to estimate from a sample

objects.text: Divide by n: variance of y 7, covariance 4.167. By n - 1: 8.4 and 5.

slides.notes:
A trap you will meet. There are two versions of variance and covariance. The population version divides by n. The sample version divides by n minus one, and it is used when you estimate from a small sample. Spreadsheets have both: VAR.P and VAR.S. NumPy divides by n by default, but pandas divides by n minus one by default.

In this course we divide by n, so the notebook and the workbook agree. When a tool gives you a different number, check which version it uses. Dividing by n, our covariance is 4.167 and the variance of y is 7. Dividing by n minus one, they are 5 and 8.4.

covariance and correlation in NumPy

runs.text: import
numpy
as
np
np.mean(x), np.var(x), np.std(x)
np.cov(x, y, bias=

objects.text: In plain words

runs.text: Lines 2 and 3: the two columns as arrays.
Line 4: mean, variance and standard deviation. np.var divides by n.
Line 5: np.cov gives a 2 by 2 matrix. bias=True divides by n. The entry in row 0, column 1 is Cov(x, y).
Line 6: np.corrcoef gives the correlation matrix. Same entry is r.
Spreadsheet: AVERAGE, VAR.P, STDEV.P, COVARIANCE.P and CORREL do the same.

slides.notes:
Here is the same work in code. Two arrays, x and y. NumPy has mean, var and std, and var divides by n. For covariance we call np.cov with bias equals True, so it divides by n, and it returns a small matrix. The covariance of x and y is the entry in row zero, column one.

np.corrcoef gives the correlation matrix in the same shape. In the spreadsheet you use AVERAGE, VAR.P, STDEV.P, COVARIANCE.P and CORREL. You will see the same numbers in both tools.

title.text:
Bridge: simulate dice with a fixed
seed so everyone gets the same rolls

runs.text: rng = np.random.default_rng(13)
rolls = rng.integers(1, 7, size=60)
rolls.mean(), rolls.var()
big = rng.integers(1, 7, size=10000)
big.mean(), big.var()

objects.text: In plain words

runs.text: Line 1: a random number generator. Seed 13 fixes the sequence.
Line 2: 60 whole numbers from 1 to 6 (7 is excluded).
Line 3: 60 rolls give a noisy mean (here 3.9667) and variance (3.1322).
Lines 4 and 5: 10,000 rolls come much closer to 3.5 and 2.9167.
Spreadsheet: the 60 rolls are fixed values, so nothing changes.

slides.notes:
Simulation means letting the computer roll the dice for us. The generator with seed thirteen gives the same sequence on every machine, so your numbers match mine. The call integers from one to seven gives whole numbers from one to six, because the upper limit is not included.

Sixty rolls give a noisy mean, here 3.9667, and variance, here 3.1322. Ten thousand rolls come much closer to 3.5 and 2.9167. In the spreadsheet we avoid the volatile RAND function and paste fixed rolls instead, so the numbers stay put.

title.text:
Where this appears in AI: a language
model gives every next token a probability

objects.alt: Where this appears in AI: a language model gives every next token a probability

objects.text: Language models of this kind output a probability mass function over the whole vocabulary.

runs.text: Published transformers end in a softmax over the vocabulary.
Llama 2 (open): 32,000 tokens in the vocabulary.
Closed products do not publish details.

slides.notes:
Here is where today appears in real systems. The published transformer design ends with one score, a logit, for every token in its vocabulary. Softmax turns those scores into a probability mass function that adds to one. The open model Llama 2, for example, has a published vocabulary of 32,000 tokens.

ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude are products built on models of this kind, but their exact details are not public. So we use the published design and open models to show the same mathematics. Next session we study how the model then chooses from this list.

title.text:
Where this appears in AI: mean and standard
deviation rescale numbers inside the model

objects.alt: Where this appears in AI: mean and standard deviation rescale numbers inside the model

objects.text: The original transformer uses layer normalisation: each vector is centred and scaled with its own mean and standard deviation.

runs.text: Layer normalisation: Ba, Kiros and Hinton, 2016.
Some newer open models use a variant (RMSNorm) that scales without centring.

slides.notes:
Expectation and variance are not only for dice. The published transformer design uses layer normalisation, a step from a 2016 paper by Ba, Kiros and Hinton. Inside a layer, each vector of numbers is shifted by its own mean and divided by its own standard deviation. That keeps the numbers in a friendly range, which helps training.

It is exactly the mean and the standard deviation you computed today, applied to a long list of numbers. Some newer open models, Llama among them, use a variant called RMSNorm that scales without centring.

Now a short activity. Open any AI assistant and give it our six pairs. Ask for the covariance and the correlation, and ask which formula it used. Then compare with your lab. Assistants sometimes make arithmetic mistakes, and sometimes divide by n minus one, which gives five instead of 4.167.

Both can be right for their own formula, so the useful skill is to know which one it used. Please use only made-up data like this, and never paste confidential data into an assistant.

title.text: Exit check: three questions

rows.text: A model gives probabilities 0.5, 0.3 and 0.1 to three words and nothing else is possible. What is wrong?
They add to 0.9. A pmf must add to exactly 1.
What is the expectation of a fair die, and can you roll it?
3.5. No: it is an average, and no face shows 3.5.
Two columns have correlation 0.02. Are they unrelated?
Not necessarily. Correlation only sees straight-line trends. Draw the scatter plot.

slides.notes:
Three questions to finish. First, three words with probabilities 0.5, 0.3 and 0.1 and nothing else possible: they add to 0.9, so something is missing, and a probability mass function must add to exactly one. Second, the expectation of a fair die is 3.5, and you cannot roll it, because it is an average.

Third, correlation near zero does not mean no relationship, because correlation only sees straight lines, so draw the scatter plot. Write your answers in your lab file.
